13:1.text: And they gave him audience unto this word, and then lifted up their voices, and said, Away with such a fellow from the earth: for it is not fit that he should live.

provenance.other: “such a fellow” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. “away with this” occurs in exactly two, of which only Luke 23:18 is a cry against a man.
provenance.significance: Noah's sentence fuses the two KJV mob-cries verbatim: the crowd before Pilate (“Away with this man, and release unto us Barabbas”) and the crowd before the Roman tribune (“Away with such a fellow from the earth: for it is not fit that he should live”). Recover either context and the chapter has already announced its own ending. Abinadi will be burned at 17:20, and the two scenes the KJV lends him are the condemnation of Jesus and the near-lynching of Paul — the two prisoners in the New Testament whose accusers demand a death the magistrate has not yet ordered. That is a great deal of freight for six words, and it is loaded before Abinadi has said anything at all.

13:1.note: “Away with this fellow, and slay him: for what have we to do with him, for he is mad.” The king's order is built out of two KJV cries and takes a word from each: “Away with this” is Luke 23:18's, and “fellow” in that construction is Acts 22:22's, where the phrase “such a fellow” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and is followed by the demand that he not be allowed to live. Noah supplies “and slay him”, which is what Acts 22:22 means. The closing charge, that Abinadi is mad, is the charge laid against Jesus at John 10:20 and against Paul by Festus at Acts 26:24, and Abinadi answers it at 13:4 the way Paul answers it at Acts 26:25.

13:3.text: Jesus saith unto her, Touch me not; for I am not yet ascended to my Father: but go to my brethren, and say unto them, I ascend unto my Father, and your Father; and to my God, and your God.

provenance.other: “touch me not” occurs in exactly one KJV verse.
provenance.alternative: Psalm 105:15 and 1 Chronicles 16:22 — “Touch not mine anointed, and do my prophets no harm” — are the obvious prophetic-immunity text, and the sense of Abinadi's sentence is theirs rather than John's.
provenance.significance: The KJV says “Touch me not” once, and the reason given there is temporal: “for I am not yet ascended to my Father.” Abinadi's reason is temporal in the same grammatical shape — “God will not suffer that I shall be destroyed at this time” — a prohibition on handling a body that is not yet finished with its errand. The two verses do opposite things with the same clause: John's forbids touch because the work is already done, Abinadi's because it is not.

13:3.note: “Touch me not, for God shall smite you if ye lay your hands upon me.” The imperative is a KJV singleton, and the verse it comes from attaches to it exactly the kind of reason Abinadi attaches: not-yet. Recorded at moderate because the substance of the claim is Psalm 105:15's prophetic immunity and only the two words are John's; a reader who prefers the psalm loses the timing but keeps the sense.

13:3.text: Then they sought to take him: but no man laid hands on him, because his hour was not yet come.

provenance.other: “his hour was not yet come” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, John 7:30 and John 8:20, and both attach it to the same fact: men reached for him and could not take him.
provenance.significance: John's formula is the Bible's one explanation of why a hostile crowd fails to seize a preacher mid-sermon, and it is a statement about a schedule, not about the crowd's strength. Mosiah 13:2-3 needs precisely that explanation — hands are laid on and withdraw — and gives it in the same terms, then spends the rest of the chapter using the reprieve: “I finish my message” (13:7, 13:9). Both narratives are counting down to a death they have already accepted.

13:3.note: “They stood forth and attempted to lay their hands on him; but he withstood them … God will not suffer that I shall be destroyed at this time.” The situation and its explanation are John 7:30's, where they “sought to take him: but no man laid hands on him, because his hour was not yet come”. What is reproduced is not wording but a doctrine of timing, and the Book of Mormon states it as a conditional on an unfinished message rather than an appointed hour — which is the difference between a prophet with a text to deliver and a Christ with a passion to reach.

13:5.text: And it came to pass, when Moses came down from mount Sinai with the two tables of testimony in Moses’ hand, when he came down from the mount, that Moses wist not that the skin of his face shone while he talked with him.

provenance.other: “the skin of his face shone” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Exodus 34:29 and 34:30, and both belong to the descent from Sinai with the second pair of tables.
provenance.significance: The comparison is not decorative, it is jurisdictional. Abinadi's face shines at the moment he is about to read the Ten Commandments aloud, and the one man in the KJV whose face shines is the man coming down the mountain with those commandments in his hand. Exodus 34:30 adds what Mosiah 13 needs next — “they were afraid to come nigh him” — which is why the priests cannot lay hands on him. What Abinadi borrows from Moses is not glory but the right to be the one holding the tables.

13:5.note: “His face shone with exceeding lustre, even as Moses did while in the mount of Sinai, while speaking with the Lord.” The Book of Mormon names its source outright, so the interest is in which Moses it names: not the ascent but the descent of Exodus 34, where the shining is a consequence of speaking with the Lord and where the people cannot come near. The 1830 “lustre” was modernized to “luster” in 1920, and the 1830 reads “even as Moses did” against 1920's “Moses'” — the first edition compares the shining to Moses's action, the modern text to Moses's face.

13:5.text: And all that sat in the council, looking stedfastly on him, saw his face as it had been the face of an angel.

provenance.alternative: Every element can be got from Exodus and from the Hebrew prophets separately; the type-scene is an inference from their co-occurrence in one order, not from any shared wording.
provenance.significance: Read Mosiah 13 beside Acts 6-7 and the sequence is the same sequence, in the same order, four times over: the accused stands before a hostile council and his face is transfigured (Acts 6:15 / Mosiah 13:5); he recites Israel's law and history at length; he calls his judges stiffnecked (Acts 7:51 / Mosiah 13:29); they are cut to the heart (Acts 7:54 / Mosiah 13:7); they kill him. Stephen is the New Testament's one martyr-by-mob-execution after a legal recital, and Abinadi is the Book of Mormon's. The catalogue records the individual verbal borrowings at 13:7 and 13:29 as links in their own right; this row is the claim that they are not four coincidences but one scene.

13:5.note: Proposed on shape rather than wording. The chapter's three strongest New Testament borrowings — “cut to the heart” at 13:7, “stiffnecked” at 13:29, and the shining face here — all come from a single ten-verse stretch of Acts, and they arrive in Acts's order. Acts 6:15 shares no phrase with Mosiah 13:5 (its face is “as it had been the face of an angel”, the Book of Mormon's shines like Moses's), so this is catalogued as figural and the Exodus 34 link above carries the verbal case.
13:5.whyNot: No verbal contact whatever at this verse, and the three constituent links are each independently explicable: the shining face is Exodus 34's, “stiffnecked” is Exodus and Deuteronomy's before it is Stephen's, and only “cut to the heart” is peculiar to Acts. A reader who declines the type-scene keeps all three links and loses only the claim that they cohere.

13:7.text: When they heard these things, they were cut to the heart, and they gnashed on him with their teeth.

provenance.other: “cut to the heart” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Acts 5:33 and Acts 7:54, and in both the hearers respond by trying to kill the speaker.
provenance.significance: The idiom exists in the KJV only in Acts, only in the Sanhedrin, and only as the prelude to a killing — at 5:33 they take counsel to slay the apostles, at 7:54 they gnash their teeth and stone Stephen. Abinadi uses it as a diagnosis of his own audience while they are deciding what to do with him, which means the borrowing carries the outcome with it. This catalogue met the same idiom at 1 Nephi 16:2, where Nephi tells his brothers the guilty take the truth to be hard “for it cutteth them to the very center”; Mosiah 13:7 is the phrase in its Acts form, and in an Acts situation.

13:7.note: “I perceive that it cuts you to your hearts, because I tell you the truth concerning your iniquities.” The KJV's two occurrences are both Luke's, both in the council, and both immediately followed by an attempt on the speaker's life; Acts 7:54 is preferred over 5:33 because the rest of the chapter borrows from the same Stephen episode (see 13:5 and 13:29). Abinadi's clause supplies the causal half that Acts leaves implicit — what cuts is the truth about their iniquities — which is Stephen's speech in one sentence.

13:8.text: And they knew that it was he which sat for alms at the Beautiful gate of the temple: and they were filled with wonder and amazement at that which had happened unto him.

provenance.other: “filled with wonder and amazement” occurs in exactly one KJV verse.
provenance.significance: Mosiah 13 goes to Acts 3 twice: for this phrase, and at 13:33 for the prophets who have spoken since the world began. In Acts the wonder and amazement belong to a crowd that has just seen a lame man walk, and Peter turns it immediately into the sermon that runs from the prophets since the world began to Moses's prophet-like-unto-me. Abinadi reverses the polarity and keeps the structure: the wonder is produced by words rather than a healing, it is mixed with anger, and it too is followed by an appeal to all the prophets since the world began. The same chapter of Acts furnishes both the reaction and the argument.

13:8.note: “My words fill you with wonder and amazement, and with anger.” The three-word collocation is a KJV singleton and the Book of Mormon reproduces the whole construction, verb included. Its one addition is the anger, which Acts 3:10 does not have and which converts a crowd's astonishment into a court's. Note that the anger belongs to the KJV's other reaction-formula, the one at 13:7: in Acts, being cut to the heart is what produces the killing, and Abinadi has just said his hearers are.

13:10.text: Which are a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ.

provenance.other: “shadow of things to come” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; “shadow of good things to come” occurs in exactly one, Hebrews 10:1; “the example and shadow” occurs in exactly one, Hebrews 8:5.
provenance.significance: The KJV uses “shadow” for typology in three places and all three are about the same thing: the law of Moses as a provisional figure of Christ. Colossians 2:17 says it of sabbaths and holy days, Hebrews 10:1 of the sacrifices, Hebrews 8:5 of the tabernacle Moses was shown in the mount. Abinadi is about to argue exactly that thesis — salvation does not come by the law, the law is a set of performances kept in remembrance, “all these things were types of things to come” (13:31) — and he opens with the KJV's own word for it. What makes 13:10 remarkable is its referent: the shadow is not a sacrifice or a feast but his own execution.

13:10.note: “What you do with me after this, shall be as a type and a shadow of things which is to come.” The phrase is Colossians 2:17's, a KJV singleton, and Paul's subject there is the law's ordinances; the pairing “type and … shadow” has no single KJV verse behind it and reads as a fusion of Colossians's “shadow” with the typological “figure” language of Romans 5:14 and Hebrews 9:24. Adjudicated here rather than at 13:31, where the same doctrine recurs in Abinadi's own now-established formula. The 1830 “things which is to come” was corrected to “things which are to come” in 1920; the singular verb is the first edition's, not the KJV's.

13:11.text: Forasmuch as ye are manifestly declared to be the epistle of Christ ministered by us, written not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God; not in tables of stone, but in fleshy tables of the heart.

provenance.other: “in tables of stone” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; “written not with ink” occurs in exactly one; “the ministration of death” occurs in exactly one. All three are 2 Corinthians 3.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's most economical borrowing and the reason the verse before it matters. 2 Corinthians 3 is the KJV's one sustained argument that the commandments engraved in stone are inferior to commandments written in the heart — and it makes that argument by way of Moses's shining face (3:7, 3:13), the very comparison Mosiah 13:5 has just drawn. So the Book of Mormon takes Paul's Moses at 13:5 and Paul's contrast at 13:11, in Paul's order, and then does what Paul's argument requires: reads the tables of stone aloud to men in whose hearts they are not written. Recover 2 Corinthians 3 and Abinadi's recital of the Decalogue is already framed as a ministration of death.

13:11.note: “I read unto you the remainder of the commandments of God, for I perceive that they are not written in your hearts.” The contrast between a law read off stone and a law written in the heart is Jeremiah 31:33's in substance and 2 Corinthians 3:3's in this form — “not in tables of stone, but in fleshy tables of the heart” — and Paul's chapter is the one that reaches it through Moses's shining face, which Mosiah 13:5 has invoked six verses earlier. The verse is doing two things at once: it explains why the commandments have to be read at all, and it convicts the priests in advance of the recital.

13:12.text: Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth.

provenance.other: The whole verse, thirty-four words, reproduced with two changes. “in the water under the earth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse.
provenance.alternative: Deuteronomy 5:8 has the same commandment in nearly the same words; see the exclusion register at this verse.
provenance.significance: The Decalogue in Mosiah 13 is Exodus 20's, not Deuteronomy 5's, and the catalogue can say so mechanically: tools/mediation-check.py returns a decisive reading for Exodus at 13:12 (“water under”, not Deuteronomy's “waters beneath”), 13:18 (no ox, no ass, no rest-clause), 13:20 (no “as the LORD thy God hath commanded thee”, and “long upon” rather than “prolonged”) and 13:24 (“nor”, not “or”), and 13:19 reproduces a creation rationale that Deuteronomy 5 does not contain at all. The one word that runs the other way is at 13:13.

13:12.note: The second commandment, verbatim from Exodus 20:4 apart from “any thing that is” thrice reduced to “things which is”. That reduction is the verse's evidence in two directions at once. It rules out Deuteronomy 5:8, which reads “waters beneath the earth” where both Exodus and Mosiah read “water under the earth” — tools/mediation-check.py returns that as the decisive point. And it is 1830 grammar rather than KJV grammar: the first edition's singular verb after a plural subject was corrected to “things which are” in 1920, at all three occurrences in this verse.

13:13.text: Thou shalt not bow down thyself to them, nor serve them: for I the LORD thy God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation of them that hate me;

provenance.other: “am a jealous God, visiting” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Exodus 20:5 and Deuteronomy 5:9. Deuteronomy 5:9 reads “bow down thyself unto them” where Exodus 20:5 reads “to them”; Mosiah 13:13 reads “unto them”.
provenance.significance: The Decalogue in Mosiah 13 is Exodus 20's, not Deuteronomy 5's, and the catalogue can say so mechanically: tools/mediation-check.py returns a decisive reading for Exodus at 13:12 (“water under”, not Deuteronomy's “waters beneath”), 13:18 (no ox, no ass, no rest-clause), 13:20 (no “as the LORD thy God hath commanded thee”, and “long upon” rather than “prolonged”) and 13:24 (“nor”, not “or”), and 13:19 reproduces a creation rationale that Deuteronomy 5 does not contain at all. The one word that runs the other way is at 13:13. Here it is one preposition, and it points at Deuteronomy: the Book of Mormon's “unto them” is Deuteronomy 5:9's word, not Exodus 20:5's. One word against four decisive readings elsewhere is not enough to move the source, and the honest description is contamination rather than choice — the two versions of the Decalogue are near enough that a text reproducing one from memory or from a reading Bible will not be uniform. The catalogue records the exception rather than smoothing it.

13:13.note: The third clause of the second commandment, twenty-three words continuous. Two departures carry information. “Unto them” agrees with Deuteronomy 5:9 against Exodus 20:5's “to them”, and is the only point in the whole Mosiah 13 Decalogue where Deuteronomy is the closer text. “Iniquities … generations” are plurals against the KJV's singulars in both versions, which is the Book of Mormon's own hand: the same pluralizing appears at 14:6, 14:8 and 14:12 in the Isaiah 53 transcription that follows this chapter.

13:14.text: And shewing mercy unto thousands of them that love me, and keep my commandments.

provenance.other: “shewing mercy unto thousands” occurs in exactly two KJV verses. Exodus 20:6 and Deuteronomy 5:10 are word-for-word identical in the KJV, so this verse cannot decide its own source; it is assigned to Exodus by the four decisive readings elsewhere in the recital.
provenance.significance: The Decalogue in Mosiah 13 is Exodus 20's, not Deuteronomy 5's, and the catalogue can say so mechanically: tools/mediation-check.py returns a decisive reading for Exodus at 13:12 (“water under”, not Deuteronomy's “waters beneath”), 13:18 (no ox, no ass, no rest-clause), 13:20 (no “as the LORD thy God hath commanded thee”, and “long upon” rather than “prolonged”) and 13:24 (“nor”, not “or”), and 13:19 reproduces a creation rationale that Deuteronomy 5 does not contain at all. The one word that runs the other way is at 13:13.

13:14.note: Fourteen words verbatim. The evidence this verse carries is orthographic: the 1830 reads “shewing”, which is the KJV's spelling, and 1920 modernized it to “showing”. The borrowing is plainer in the first edition than in the current text, which is the general argument for using 1830 as the running text (CONVENTIONS §8).

13:15.text: Thou shalt not take the name of the LORD thy God in vain; for the LORD will not hold him guiltless that taketh his name in vain.

provenance.other: “hold him guiltless that taketh” occurs in exactly two KJV verses. Twenty-seven words continuous, the longest unbroken run in the chapter and one of the longest outside a transcribed Isaiah block. Exodus 20:7 and Deuteronomy 5:11 differ only in punctuation, so this verse does not decide its own source either.
provenance.significance: The Decalogue in Mosiah 13 is Exodus 20's, not Deuteronomy 5's, and the catalogue can say so mechanically: tools/mediation-check.py returns a decisive reading for Exodus at 13:12 (“water under”, not Deuteronomy's “waters beneath”), 13:18 (no ox, no ass, no rest-clause), 13:20 (no “as the LORD thy God hath commanded thee”, and “long upon” rather than “prolonged”) and 13:24 (“nor”, not “or”), and 13:19 reproduces a creation rationale that Deuteronomy 5 does not contain at all. The one word that runs the other way is at 13:13.

13:15.note: The third commandment entire, twenty-seven words with no departure at all — above Skousen's sixteen-word threshold, and the only verse of Mosiah 13 that is. It is worth saying plainly what a run of this length means for the chapter as a whole: Abinadi is not alluding to the Decalogue, he is reading it out of an English Bible printed in 1611, and the Book of Mormon says so in its own terms at 13:11 (“I read unto you”).

13:16.text: Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy.

provenance.other: “Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; Deuteronomy 5:12 reads “Keep the sabbath day to sanctify it”, which is decisive against Deuteronomy.
provenance.significance: The Decalogue in Mosiah 13 is Exodus 20's, not Deuteronomy 5's, and the catalogue can say so mechanically: tools/mediation-check.py returns a decisive reading for Exodus at 13:12 (“water under”, not Deuteronomy's “waters beneath”), 13:18 (no ox, no ass, no rest-clause), 13:20 (no “as the LORD thy God hath commanded thee”, and “long upon” rather than “prolonged”) and 13:24 (“nor”, not “or”), and 13:19 reproduces a creation rationale that Deuteronomy 5 does not contain at all. The one word that runs the other way is at 13:13. This verse is a fifth decisive point and the cleanest of them: Deuteronomy's fourth commandment does not begin with “Remember” at all.

13:16.note: Eight words verbatim from Exodus 20:8, and the choice of version is settled by the first word. Deuteronomy 5:12 has “Keep the sabbath day to sanctify it, as the LORD thy God hath commanded thee”; the Book of Mormon has Exodus's imperative and Exodus's infinitive. The 1830 hyphenates “sabbath-day” here and at 13:19, an 1830 compositor's convention rather than a KJV reading.

13:17.text: Six days shalt thou labour, and do all thy work:

provenance.other: “Six days shalt thou labour” occurs in exactly one KJV verse: Deuteronomy 5:13 inverts the auxiliary, ‘Six days thou shalt labour’.
provenance.significance: The Decalogue in Mosiah 13 is Exodus 20's, not Deuteronomy 5's, and the catalogue can say so mechanically: tools/mediation-check.py returns a decisive reading for Exodus at 13:12 (“water under”, not Deuteronomy's “waters beneath”), 13:18 (no ox, no ass, no rest-clause), 13:20 (no “as the LORD thy God hath commanded thee”, and “long upon” rather than “prolonged”) and 13:24 (“nor”, not “or”), and 13:19 reproduces a creation rationale that Deuteronomy 5 does not contain at all. The one word that runs the other way is at 13:13.

13:17.note: Nine words verbatim, the sabbath commandment's premise — and a sixth decisive point against Deuteronomy, which was missed on the first pass because the two verses look identical: Deuteronomy 5:13 reads ‘Six days thou shalt labour’, and the Book of Mormon has Exodus's word order. The only other departure is the 1830's American “labor” for the KJV's “labour” — an 1830 spelling, not a variant reading, and a reminder that the first edition modernizes orthography in one direction while preserving it in another (“shewing” at 13:14, “lustre” at 13:5).

13:18.text: But the seventh day is the sabbath of the LORD thy God: in it thou shalt not do any work, thou, nor thy son, nor thy daughter, thy manservant, nor thy maidservant, nor thy cattle, nor thy stranger that is within thy gates:

provenance.other: “nor thy stranger that is within thy gates” occurs in exactly two KJV verses. Deuteronomy 5:14 inserts “nor thine ox, nor thine ass, nor any of” before the cattle and appends “that thy manservant and thy maidservant may rest as well as thou”. Mosiah 13:18 has neither.
provenance.significance: The Decalogue in Mosiah 13 is Exodus 20's, not Deuteronomy 5's, and the catalogue can say so mechanically: tools/mediation-check.py returns a decisive reading for Exodus at 13:12 (“water under”, not Deuteronomy's “waters beneath”), 13:18 (no ox, no ass, no rest-clause), 13:20 (no “as the LORD thy God hath commanded thee”, and “long upon” rather than “prolonged”) and 13:24 (“nor”, not “or”), and 13:19 reproduces a creation rationale that Deuteronomy 5 does not contain at all. The one word that runs the other way is at 13:13.

13:18.note: The household list reproduced in Exodus's shorter form, and this is the second decisive point against Deuteronomy: tools/mediation-check.py returns both of Deuteronomy 5:14's expansions as absent here. The one substantive change is at the head of the verse — Exodus's “the seventh day is the sabbath … in it thou shalt not do any work” becomes an apposition, “the seventh day, the sabbath of the Lord thy God, thou shalt not do any work” — which is the kind of compression a reader makes aloud, not a variant.

13:19.text: For in six days the LORD made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that in them is, and rested the seventh day: wherefore the LORD blessed the sabbath day, and hallowed it.

provenance.other: “wherefore the LORD blessed the sabbath day” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Deuteronomy 5:15 gives a wholly different rationale for the sabbath — the deliverance from Egypt — and contains no creation clause at all.
provenance.significance: The Decalogue in Mosiah 13 is Exodus 20's, not Deuteronomy 5's, and the catalogue can say so mechanically: tools/mediation-check.py returns a decisive reading for Exodus at 13:12 (“water under”, not Deuteronomy's “waters beneath”), 13:18 (no ox, no ass, no rest-clause), 13:20 (no “as the LORD thy God hath commanded thee”, and “long upon” rather than “prolonged”) and 13:24 (“nor”, not “or”), and 13:19 reproduces a creation rationale that Deuteronomy 5 does not contain at all. The one word that runs the other way is at 13:13. This verse is the strongest of the five points, because it is not a difference of wording but of content: Deuteronomy's fourth commandment grounds the sabbath in the Exodus, Exodus's grounds it in the creation, and Mosiah 13:19 grounds it in the creation.

13:19.note: Exodus 20:11 with one omission that is worth noticing: the Book of Mormon drops “and rested the seventh day”, so the verse moves straight from the six days of making to the blessing of the sabbath. The omitted clause is the only anthropomorphism in the commandment, and its absence leaves the sabbath grounded in what God made rather than in what he did afterwards. Whether that is deliberate or a skip in dictation the catalogue cannot say; it is the single largest departure in the whole recital.

13:20.text: Honour thy father and thy mother: that thy days may be long upon the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee.

provenance.other: “that thy days may be long upon the land” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Deuteronomy 5:16 adds “as the LORD thy God hath commanded thee” and reads “thy days may be prolonged, and that it may go well with thee”. Mosiah 13:20 has Exodus's “long upon” and neither addition.
provenance.significance: The Decalogue in Mosiah 13 is Exodus 20's, not Deuteronomy 5's, and the catalogue can say so mechanically: tools/mediation-check.py returns a decisive reading for Exodus at 13:12 (“water under”, not Deuteronomy's “waters beneath”), 13:18 (no ox, no ass, no rest-clause), 13:20 (no “as the LORD thy God hath commanded thee”, and “long upon” rather than “prolonged”) and 13:24 (“nor”, not “or”), and 13:19 reproduces a creation rationale that Deuteronomy 5 does not contain at all. The one word that runs the other way is at 13:13.

13:20.note: Twenty-one words continuous, and the third decisive point against Deuteronomy — two of them in one verse, since Mosiah lacks both of Deuteronomy 5:16's expansions. The 1830 “Honor” for the KJV's “Honour” is American orthography of the same kind as “labor” at 13:17, and carries no textual weight.

provenance.other: Four words, identical in Exodus 20:13, Deuteronomy 5:17, Matthew 5:21, Matthew 19:18 (as “do no murder”), Mark 10:19, Luke 18:20, Romans 13:9 and James 2:11. No English version of any date reads otherwise.
provenance.significance: Recorded for completeness of the recital rather than for evidence. The commandment's placement is the finding, not its wording: Mosiah 13:21-23 gives kill, then adultery and theft together, then false witness, which is Exodus's order and not Romans 13:9's (adultery, kill, steal) or Matthew 19:18's (murder, adultery, steal, false witness). See the exclusions at 13:22.

13:21.note: The sixth commandment. Four words that are the same in every English Bible and in every New Testament citation of the Decalogue, so kjvSpecific is 'no' and the verse can carry no version argument on its own. What it does carry is sequence: it stands where Exodus puts it, before adultery and theft, and it is that ordering which excludes the two New Testament lists the machine stream proposes at 13:22.

provenance.other: The n-gram stream ranks Matthew 19:18 and Romans 13:9 above Exodus here, because both put “Thou shalt not commit adultery, Thou shalt not steal” in one verse where Exodus splits them across two. That is an artifact of versification, not of wording.
provenance.significance: A worked example of ADJUDICATING §4's warning that a long n-gram run means nothing on its own. The eight-word match with Romans 13:9 is real and it is worthless: Romans has the commandments in a different order (adultery, kill, steal), Matthew 19:18 uses “do no murder” for the commandment Mosiah 13:21 gives as “kill”, and both are lists inside an argument rather than a recital. The Book of Mormon is running Exodus 20 straight through, and the two verses fell into one only because whoever divided Mosiah into verses in 1879 put them there.

13:22.note: The seventh and eighth commandments, four words each, verbatim. Both New Testament candidates are excluded on order and on the preceding verse: Mosiah 13:21 reads “Thou shalt not kill”, which is Exodus's and Romans's word but not Matthew's, and Mosiah's sequence kill → adultery → steal → false witness is Exodus's and neither of theirs. See the exclusion register.

13:23.text: Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour.

provenance.other: Identical in Exodus 20:16 and, but for “vain” for “false”, in Deuteronomy 5:20.
provenance.significance: The Decalogue in Mosiah 13 is Exodus 20's, not Deuteronomy 5's, and the catalogue can say so mechanically: tools/mediation-check.py returns a decisive reading for Exodus at 13:12 (“water under”, not Deuteronomy's “waters beneath”), 13:18 (no ox, no ass, no rest-clause), 13:20 (no “as the LORD thy God hath commanded thee”, and “long upon” rather than “prolonged”) and 13:24 (“nor”, not “or”), and 13:19 reproduces a creation rationale that Deuteronomy 5 does not contain at all. The one word that runs the other way is at 13:13.

13:23.note: The ninth commandment, verbatim but for the 1830's American “neighbor” against the KJV's “neighbour”. Deuteronomy 5:20 reads “vain witness” where Exodus and Mosiah read “false witness”, which is a fourth small point in Exodus's favour, though not one the mediation tool counts as decisive because the surrounding words are identical.

13:24.text: Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour’s house, thou shalt not covet thy neighbour’s wife, nor his manservant, nor his maidservant, nor his ox, nor his ass, nor any thing that is thy neighbour’s.

provenance.other: “nor his ox, nor his ass” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Deuteronomy 5:21 reverses the order (wife before house), begins the second half “Neither shalt thou desire”, adds “his field”, and links the list with “or” where Exodus uses “nor”. Mosiah 13:24 follows Exodus at every one of those points.
provenance.significance: The Decalogue in Mosiah 13 is Exodus 20's, not Deuteronomy 5's, and the catalogue can say so mechanically: tools/mediation-check.py returns a decisive reading for Exodus at 13:12 (“water under”, not Deuteronomy's “waters beneath”), 13:18 (no ox, no ass, no rest-clause), 13:20 (no “as the LORD thy God hath commanded thee”, and “long upon” rather than “prolonged”) and 13:24 (“nor”, not “or”), and 13:19 reproduces a creation rationale that Deuteronomy 5 does not contain at all. The one word that runs the other way is at 13:13. The tenth commandment is where the two versions differ most, and it is the fourth and last decisive reading: three separate “nor”-for-“or” agreements with Exodus, plus house-before-wife, plus no field.

13:24.note: The tenth commandment entire, thirty words, the closing verse of the recital and the one where Deuteronomy is furthest away. Every distinguishing feature of Deuteronomy 5:21 is absent and every feature of Exodus 20:17 is present. The 1830 reads “nor any thing that is thy neighbor's”, two words, exactly as the KJV prints it; 1920 closed it to “anything”, which is the only place in the chapter where a modern edition has moved the text away from its source.

13:26.text: And the king of Israel said unto Jehoshaphat, There is yet one man, Micaiah the son of Imlah, by whom we may enquire of the LORD: but I hate him; for he doth not prophesy good concerning me, but evil. And Jehoshaphat said, Let not the king say so.

provenance.other: “prophesy good concerning me” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; the same king repeats the complaint at 1 Kings 22:18, “Did I not tell thee that he would prophesy no good concerning me, but evil?”
provenance.significance: 1 Kings 22 is the KJV's one full-dress scene of a king with a court of house prophets who tell him what he wants and one outsider who does not, and it is the scene Mosiah 11-17 has been staging since Noah appointed his own priests. Micaiah is fetched, contradicts four hundred paid prophets, is struck by one of them and imprisoned on bread and water until the king returns in peace — and the king does not return. Abinadi is the same figure at the same court, and the phrase he uses to describe his own errand is the phrase Ahab uses to describe Micaiah's.

13:26.note: “The Lord would not have caused me to come forth and to prophesy evil concerning this people.” The collocation of prophesying and “evil concerning” a hearer is Ahab's, from a KJV singleton, and it is a king's word for a prophet he intends to imprison. Recorded at moderate because the shared string is short and the sense is the natural one; what raises it above coincidence is that Mosiah 11-13 has already assembled the rest of 1 Kings 22 — a king, a bought priesthood, a lone prophet summoned and condemned.

13:27.text: And by him all that believe are justified from all things, from which ye could not be justified by the law of Moses.

provenance.other: “by the law of Moses” occurs in exactly one KJV verse.
provenance.significance: Abinadi is answering a claim his hearers have made — “ye have said that salvation cometh by the law of Moses” — and the sentence he puts in their mouths is the sentence Paul denies at Antioch in Pisidia, in the KJV's only occurrence of the phrase. Recover Acts 13 and the whole shape of Mosiah 13:27-33 is there: a synagogue address that recites Israel's history, denies that the law justifies, and turns on the prophets. Paul is even answering the same objection in the same order, law first and prophets after.

13:27.note: “Ye have said that salvation cometh by the law of Moses … the time shall come when it shall no more be expedient to keep the law of Moses.” The formula is a KJV singleton and it is Paul's, from the one verse in the Bible that says what cannot be got by the law of Moses. Abinadi's addition is temporal rather than doctrinal: he does not abolish the law, he dates it — keep it “as yet”, and the time shall come. That is the Book of Mormon's characteristic move with Pauline material, and it recurs at 13:28.

13:28.text: And not only so, but we also joy in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, by whom we have now received the atonement.

provenance.other: “The atonement” occurs in exactly six KJV verses; five are Levitical, of a rite performed by a priest, and Romans 5:11 is the only one where it is a thing received through Jesus Christ.
provenance.alternative: The word is ordinary English theological vocabulary by 1829 and needs no verse behind it; Abinadi may simply be using the noun.
provenance.significance: The KJV's word for the thing Christ does is not “atonement” but “propitiation” or “reconciliation” — the King James translators used “atonement” once in the New Testament, at Romans 5:11, and the Revised Version removed it there. So a text that says “the atonement which God himself shall make” is using a word whose Christological sense exists in exactly one verse of the English Bible, and in no Greek New Testament. The Book of Mormon then goes further than Romans does, and makes God himself the one who makes it — which is the doctrine 13:34 states outright.

13:28.note: “Were it not for the atonement which God himself shall make for the sins and iniquities of his people.” Recorded as an echo, not an allusion: nothing is reproduced but the noun. It is recorded at all because of where the noun comes from. In the KJV the atonement is something a priest makes with a bullock, five times over, and once it is something believers receive through Christ; Mosiah 13:28 has the Levitical syntax (an atonement is made, for sins, for a people) with the Christological referent, which is precisely the fusion Abinadi's whole argument about the law is performing.

13:29.text: Ye stiffnecked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, ye do always resist the Holy Ghost: as your fathers did, so do ye.

provenance.other: “Stiffnecked” occurs in exactly nine KJV verses. Eight are God or Moses describing Israel in the third person or the second person plural at Sinai; Acts 7:51 is the only one where a man on trial says it to the faces of the men trying him.
provenance.significance: The word is Exodus's, but the speech-act is Stephen's, and the difference is the whole point. In Exodus and Deuteronomy “stiffnecked” is a divine verdict reported by a narrator; in Acts 7:51 it is the last sentence of a defendant's recital of the law before his judges, and the next verse but three has them cut to the heart. Mosiah 13 does both: it puts the word in a recital of the law given at Sinai (which is where the word belongs) and in the mouth of a man on trial who has already told his judges they are cut to the heart (which is where Stephen puts it). See the type-scene link at 13:5.

13:29.note: “They were a stiffnecked people, quick to do iniquity, and slow to remember the Lord their God.” The adjective is Sinai's, and Abinadi applies it to the generation that received the law rather than to his hearers — which is exactly Stephen's rhetorical structure, since Acts 7:51's “as your fathers did, so do ye” is what makes a historical charge a present one. Note the second half of the sentence: “slow to remember” inverts the KJV's “slow to anger”, which is God's attribute in Exodus 34:6 — the chapter Mosiah 13:5 has already been in.

13:29.text: Wherefore then serveth the law? It was added because of transgressions, till the seed should come to whom the promise was made; and it was ordained by angels in the hand of a mediator.

provenance.other: “Added because of transgressions” occurs in exactly one KJV verse.
provenance.alternative: The reasoning is also Hebrews's and, in a different key, Acts 15:10's yoke “which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear”; nothing here requires Galatians in particular beyond the question-and-answer form.
provenance.significance: Galatians 3:19 asks the question Mosiah 13:29 answers — wherefore then serveth the law? — and answers it the same way, that the law was an interim measure imposed because of the people who received it, holding until something else arrives. Paul's terminus is the seed to whom the promise was made; Abinadi's, two verses earlier, is the time when it shall no more be expedient to keep the law of Moses. The Book of Mormon has taken Paul's temporal argument about the law and moved it six centuries earlier, so that the law's expiry is announced by a prophet inside the dispensation it governs.

13:29.note: “It was expedient that there should be a law given to the children of Israel, yea, even a very strict law: for they were a stiffnecked people.” The proposition is Galatians 3:19's — a law added, on account of the failure of those who receive it, until a term — in the KJV's one verse that states it. What Abinadi supplies that Paul does not is the content of the failure: Paul says transgressions, Abinadi says stiffneckedness, which is the Sinai narrative's own diagnosis and lets the two halves of the verse come from Exodus and Galatians at once.

13:30.text: Which stood only in meats and drinks, and divers washings, and carnal ordinances, imposed on them until the time of reformation.

provenance.other: “Carnal ordinances” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Hebrews 9:10's ordinances “stood only in meats and drinks, and divers washings” and were “imposed on them until the time of reformation”.
provenance.alternative: “Ordinances” and “performances” are ordinary period vocabulary for ceremonial law and the phrase “law of performances” has no KJV source at all.
provenance.significance: Hebrews 9:10 is the KJV's one definition of what the Mosaic ordinances actually were and how long they were to last: outward observances, imposed until a stated terminus. Mosiah 13:30 gives the same definition in the same two parts — what they consisted of (performances and ordinances, observed strictly from day to day) and what they were for (to keep them in remembrance) — and 13:27 has already supplied the terminus. Set beside the shadow language of 13:10, the exposition is a compressed Epistle to the Hebrews: the law is a shadow, its ordinances are provisional, and what they figure is the atonement.

13:30.note: “A law of performances and of ordinances, a law which they were to observe strictly, from day to day, to keep them in remembrance of God.” No phrase is reproduced; the link is to Hebrews's account of the ceremonial law, whose defining KJV term — “carnal ordinances”, a singleton — sits in the verse that also gives the ordinances an expiry date. The Book of Mormon's one addition is the purpose clause: Hebrews says the ordinances could not make the worshipper perfect, Abinadi says what they could do, which is keep a forgetful people in remembrance.

13:32.text: And when he had looked round about on them with anger, being grieved for the hardness of their hearts, he saith unto the man, Stretch forth thine hand. And he stretched it out: and his hand was restored whole as the other.

provenance.other: “Hardness of their hearts” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The second person form, “hardness of your hearts”, is Matthew 19:8 and Mark 10:5, and the Book of Mormon uses each in its correct grammatical setting throughout the corpus.
provenance.significance: The phrase's fifth appearance in this catalogue and its first in Mosiah, so the link is written rather than excluded (ADJUDICATING §4, across a book boundary). What is new here is the object of the hardness: at 1 Nephi 2:18 and 7:8 it is Nephi's brothers refusing him, at Jarom 1:3 it is a people refusing prophets, and at Mosiah 13:32 it is Israel at Sinai failing to understand its own law. That extends a family idiom into an argument about the law of Moses — the law was not understood because of the hardness of their hearts — which is what Mark 3:5 is about too, since the hardness there is a synagogue's objection to a healing on the sabbath.

13:32.note: “They did not all understand the law; and this because of the hardness of their hearts.” Five words from a KJV singleton, in the third person, which is the grammatically correct form for hearts belonging to a third party — Matthew 19:8's “your” is what a speaker uses to his hearers, and Abinadi is talking about the fathers, not the priests. The immediate context in Mark is a sabbath dispute in a synagogue, four verses after a dispute about what the law permits on the sabbath, which is the subject Mosiah 13 has just spent eight verses reciting.

13:33.text: Whom the heaven must receive until the times of restitution of all things, which God hath spoken by the mouth of all his holy prophets since the world began.

provenance.other: “Since the world began” occurs in exactly four KJV verses; two are Luke's formula for the prophets (Luke 1:70, Acts 3:21), one is about a blind man (John 9:32) and one is Paul's about a mystery (Romans 16:25).
provenance.significance: Peter's sermon in Acts 3 runs prophets-since-the-world-began straight into Moses's prophet-like-unto-me, in that order and in consecutive verses. Mosiah 13:33 runs the same two clauses in the reverse order, Moses first and then all the prophets since the world began, and puts both inside a single rhetorical question. The reversal is the finding: Peter argues forward from Moses to the prophets to establish that Jesus is the one foretold; Abinadi argues backward from Moses to the whole line to establish that they were all saying one thing. Add 13:8's borrowing from Acts 3:10 and this chapter has taken its crowd's reaction, its prophetic warrant and its Mosaic warrant from a single page of Acts.

13:33.note: “All the prophets which have prophesied ever since the world began.” Luke's formula, in the KJV only at Luke 1:70 and Acts 3:21, and Acts 3:21 is the one that stands beside a citation of Deuteronomy 18 — which is what the first half of Mosiah 13:33 supplies. The 1830 “prophets which have prophesied” was changed to “who” in 1920; “which” is the KJV's relative for persons and the first edition preserves it.

13:33.text: The LORD thy God will raise up unto thee a Prophet from the midst of thee, of thy brethren, like unto me; unto him ye shall hearken;

provenance.route: Deuteronomy 18:15, mediated by Acts 3:22 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: tools/mediation-check.py returns no decisive point: Mosiah 13:33 reproduces neither Deuteronomy 18:15's wording (“raise up unto thee a Prophet from the midst of thee”) nor Acts 3:22's (“For Moses truly said unto the fathers”). It is a summary, not a citation.
provenance.alternative: Moses is credited with prophecies of the Messiah elsewhere in the Book of Mormon without Deuteronomy 18 being in view, and the verse may be pointing at nothing more specific than the Pentateuch.
provenance.significance: The catalogue's usual finding at Deuteronomy 18 is that the Book of Mormon has Acts's form rather than Deuteronomy's — 1 Nephi 22:20 quotes the passage outright and is decisively the Acts form. Mosiah 13:33 cannot be decided that way, because it quotes nothing. What survives the test is the frame: the claim that Moses prophesied of the Messiah, stated next to the claim that all the prophets since the world began did the same, is the argument of Acts 3:21-24 and not of Deuteronomy 18, where the prophet like unto Moses is a standing office and no messiah is in view.

13:33.note: Hardy's apparatus cross-references Deuteronomy 18:15-18 here, and the reference is right about what the verse means while there is nothing in it to test verbally. The mediation is recorded as OT-via-NT on the strength of the company the claim keeps rather than on wording: it stands immediately beside Acts 3:21's formula for the prophets, in the New Testament's own order of argument, and the messianic reading of Deuteronomy 18 that Abinadi assumes is the reading Acts 3:22-26 supplies. Catalogued as an echo, at moderate, with the wording test recorded as inconclusive rather than passed.

13:34.text: But made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men:

provenance.other: “Took upon him the form of” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and “the form of a servant” in exactly one — both Philippians 2:7.
provenance.significance: The hymn in Philippians 2 is the New Testament's one statement that a divine being took a human form, and it is the passage every subsequent doctrine of incarnation is built out of. Abinadi's sentence is that doctrine in its strongest possible form — not a son sent, but “God himself” coming down and taking the form of man — and it reaches it by keeping Philippians's verb and changing its noun from servant to man. The change is not a softening. Philippians 2:7's point is the humiliation of the form taken; Mosiah 13:34 keeps the descent (“come down among the children of men”) and adds what Philippians reserves for after the resurrection, going forth in mighty power.

13:34.note: “God himself should come down among the children of men, and take upon him the form of man.” The construction is a KJV singleton and the Book of Mormon reproduces five of its six words, substituting “man” for “a servant”. This is the doctrinal hinge of Abinadi's trial — it is what he will be executed for at 17:8 — and it is stated in Paul's words. Note that Philippians 2:7's other half, “made in the likeness of men”, is answered by the Book of Mormon's “among the children of men”, which relocates the likeness into the company.

13:35.text: He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth: he is brought as a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before her shearers is dumb, so he openeth not his mouth.

provenance.other: “Oppressed, and he was afflicted” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The pairing of the two verbs in that order occurs nowhere else in the KJV.
provenance.significance: This is the seam. Mosiah 13 ends by naming the two things the prophets said of the Messiah — the resurrection of the dead, and that he should be oppressed and afflicted — and the second is a quotation from the chapter Abinadi then recites in full. Chapter 14 is Isaiah 53 word for word, and it opens at 14:1 with an addition the KJV does not have, “Yea, even doth not Isaiah say”; so 13:35 supplies Isaiah's words without his name and 14:1 supplies his name. The catalogue's mechanical collation of chapter 14 cannot see this, because it compares verse against verse; the transition is only visible from 13:35, and it is the reason the two chapters are one speech.

13:35.note: “He, himself, should be oppressed and afflicted.” Two verbs from a KJV singleton, in the singleton's order, and they are the first words of Isaiah 53 to appear in Abinadi's speech — twelve verses of Isaiah 53 follow immediately as Mosiah 14. Read as the last sentence of chapter 13 it is a summary of the prophets; read as the first move of chapter 14 it is the citation formula. The 1830's heavy comma pointing, “he, himself, should be oppressed”, throws the weight onto the identity of the sufferer, which is the question chapter 15 opens by answering.
